The Viet Minh, the League for the Independence of Vietnam, was the front that Hồ Chí Minh founded in 1941 to win Vietnam's independence from France and Japan. It was led by the Indochinese Communist Party but drew in nationalists of many kinds.

It started in the hills of Tonkin near the Chinese border. In 1944 Võ Nguyên Giáp formed its first armed unit of a few dozen men. When Japan took full control of French Indochina in March 1945, the Viet Minh grew fast, helped by anger over the famine in the north, and its fighters seized rice stores for the hungry.

After Japan surrendered, the Viet Minh took power in the August Revolution, and on 2 September 1945 Hồ Chí Minh declared the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi. The French came back, and the First Indochina War began in December 1946. The Viet Minh also killed rivals, among them leaders of the Hòa Hảo sect.

In 1951 it was merged into a wider front, but the name stuck for the communist forces until their victory at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954.
